inputs.need:
I am the clinical nurse specialist for the ICU follow-up clinic at a regional hospital with a 24-bed mixed medical and surgical intensive care unit. Since March 2025 the families of patients ventilated for more than 72 hours have been offered a paper diary to write in each day, with a one-page guide on what to write and a nurse who checks in twice a week. About half of eligible families take one. At our 3-month follow-up clinic we see patients with nightmares, flashbacks and gaps in memory, and relatives who say they cannot stop replaying the admission.

The unit's education committee has asked me to write a narrative review of family-led diaries and post-intensive care syndrome, in patients and in relatives, to support a unit guideline and a teaching day in spring 2027. I want to know whether diaries written mainly by families, rather than by staff, change post-traumatic stress, anxiety and depression symptoms; when the diary should be read with the patient; what harms have been reported (distress on reading, privacy, photographs); and how diary programmes are run in practice, including who gets offered one.

I also want the review to be honest about how strong the evidence is, because some colleagues treat diaries as proven and others see them as a nice extra. The work has to fit protected time and the hospital library service, with no research funding.

records.title: Diaries written by relatives versus usual care after prolonged mechanical ventilation: a randomised trial of post-traumatic stress symptoms at three months
records.authors: Lindqvist-Obuya M, Harcourt-Ndiaye P, Sato-Brennan K
records.abstract: Background: diaries kept during intensive care may help patients make sense of gaps in memory. Methods: 164 adults ventilated for at least 72 hours in three units were randomised to a diary written mainly by relatives with nurse support, or to usual care; the diary was read with the patient at a nurse visit one month after discharge. The primary outcome was a post-traumatic stress symptom score above the screening threshold at three months. Results: 14 of 81 patients in the diary group and 23 of 83 in the usual care group scored above the threshold (17 versus 28 percent). Anxiety and depression scores did not differ. Loss to follow-up was 19 percent. Conclusions: a relative-written diary was followed by fewer patients with high post-traumatic stress symptoms; the trial was not powered for secondary outcomes.

records.title: Staff-written and family-written intensive care diaries: a systematic review of effects on psychological outcomes in patients and relatives
records.authors: Ferreira-Abiodun C, Nakagawa-Holm T, Brandvold-Essien R, Mistry-Llorente A
records.abstract: We searched four databases to 2022 for controlled studies of intensive care diaries that reported post-traumatic stress, anxiety or depression in patients or relatives. Eleven studies, five of them randomised, were included. In patients, pooled post-traumatic stress symptoms were lower with diaries (standardised mean difference -0.31), but the effect was not seen when the three studies at high risk of bias were removed. In relatives, two studies reported fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms and one found no difference. Only three studies described diaries written mainly by families. Heterogeneity in the timing of diary reading and in outcome instruments was substantial, and certainty was rated low.

records.title: Writing to someone who cannot answer: relatives' accounts of keeping a diary in intensive care
records.abstract: We held in-depth conversations with 19 relatives who had kept a diary for a family member in intensive care. Relatives described the diary as a place to put fear and hope, and as something to do when they felt powerless at the bedside. Several stopped writing when the patient deteriorated and restarted only after discharge. Some worried about what the patient would think of entries written on the worst days, and four had removed pages before handing the diary over. Relatives valued a short guide and a nurse who asked about the diary; they disliked being told what to write. Findings come from one hospital and from relatives who agreed to talk.

records.title: Distress on first reading an intensive care diary: an observational study of 96 survivors at a follow-up clinic
records.authors: Achterberg-Salas N, Kowalewski-Otieno B, Dunmore-Ito H
records.abstract: We asked 96 survivors to rate distress before and after first reading their diary with a nurse at a follow-up visit. Median distress rose from 2 to 4 on a 10-point scale during reading and returned to baseline within a week for 88 of 96 patients. Eight patients reported intrusive memories after reading, and six of them had high post-traumatic stress scores before reading. Photographs caused more distress than text for 21 patients. Reading with a nurse was preferred by 71 patients. The authors recommend screening for post-traumatic stress before the first reading and offering to hold back photographs until the patient asks for them.

records.title: A family diary programme and post-traumatic stress symptoms in relatives: a before-after comparison in two units
records.abstract: Two intensive care units introduced a diary programme in which relatives wrote daily with nurse prompts. We compared relatives of patients admitted in the 12 months before the change (n = 88) and the 12 months after it (n = 94), measuring post-traumatic stress symptoms 90 days after discharge or death. Symptoms above the screening threshold were reported by 36 percent of relatives before and 27 percent after. The difference was smaller when relatives of patients who died were excluded. Response to the 90-day questionnaire was 61 percent before and 58 percent after, and responders were more often spouses than adult children.

records.title: Recommendations for intensive care diaries: a consensus statement from a regional critical care network
records.authors: Regional Critical Care Network Diary Working Group
records.abstract: A panel of 14 nurses, physicians, psychologists and former patients reviewed published studies and local experience of intensive care diaries and agreed nine recommendations over three modified Delphi rounds. The panel recommends offering diaries to patients ventilated for more than 72 hours, encouraging relatives to write, giving a short written guide, agreeing rules on photographs and confidentiality, and reading the diary with a trained clinician after discharge. It makes no recommendation on staff-written versus family-written entries because the evidence was judged insufficient. The panel notes that diary programmes often lapse when the lead nurse leaves the unit.

records.title: Who receives an intensive care diary? Uptake by language, age and family presence across 1,120 eligible admissions
records.authors: Haddad-Whitcombe R, Osei-Lundgren M, Petrov-Achebe D
records.abstract: We reviewed diary uptake in 1,120 eligible admissions to four intensive care units over two years. A diary was started in 54 percent of admissions. Uptake was 31 percent when the family's main language differed from the unit's language, 38 percent for patients without a regular visitor, and 61 percent otherwise. Diaries were rarely offered to families who could visit only at night. Units with a named diary nurse had higher uptake than units without one. The authors recommend translated guides, an offer at the first family meeting, and recording who is offered a diary as well as who accepts it.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level: one randomised trial, one systematic review, two observational studies, one before-after comparison, one qualitative study and one consensus statement. The single trial of relative-written diaries found fewer patients above the post-traumatic stress threshold at three months, but the review's pooled effect in patients was fragile to risk of bias and included only three family-written diary studies. Effects in relatives rest on one uncontrolled comparison and mixed controlled results. First reading raises distress briefly and can trigger intrusive memories in patients who already have high symptoms. Uptake is lower for families with a different language or no regular visitor, and programmes lapse when the lead nurse leaves. A narrative review can state these findings with their certainty; it cannot settle whether family-written diaries work better than staff-written ones.
response.gradeRationale: One moderate-sized trial and a review whose pooled effect disappears when high-risk studies are removed, with indirectness for family-written diaries and imprecision in relatives; certainty that family-led diaries reduce post-traumatic stress symptoms is low, and very low for relatives.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.

steps.note: Appraisal of the seven retrieved records (S13 dispatches it to the appraisal mapper on the production scan path). Every passage is an exact substring of the cited abstract and every number in a claim appears in it. The certainty is the appraisal's own value over inspected records (G1).

contexts: unit guideline and teaching day, spring 2027
response.reading: Family diaries sit between the intensive care stay and the follow-up clinic: relatives write during the stay, and the diary is meant to help the patient rebuild a coherent account of what happened when it is read later. The retrieved evidence links diaries to fewer patients with high post-traumatic stress symptoms in one trial, but the pooled effect is fragile and almost no study isolates family-written entries. Reading is itself an exposure with a short-lived distress cost and a risk for patients who already have high symptoms. Who is offered a diary depends on language and on family presence, and programmes depend on a lead nurse.

response.rationale: The unit needs a readable, critical synthesis that supports a guideline and a teaching day, covering effects, harms and programme delivery across trials, observational and experience studies. A narrative review with a documented librarian-supported search, reported against SANRA, fits that purpose and the 40 approved hours. A new systematic review with meta-analysis would largely repeat the 2023 review (c2) and could not resolve the family-written question from three studies; the harms (c3) and uptake findings (c4) are better handled in narrative form. The best effect estimate (c1) is presented with its limits.

response.whyNotMoreComplex: A systematic review with pooling would add precision that the evidence cannot support and would take several times the approved hours; the guideline needs a clear account of what is known and how certain it is, which a structured narrative review provides.

store.title: Family-led intensive care diaries and post-intensive care syndrome: a narrative review for a unit guideline

response.overview: A narrative review, reported against SANRA, of family-led intensive care diaries and post-intensive care syndrome in adult patients and relatives, built on a documented librarian-supported search and organised in three parts: effects, harms of reading, and programme delivery and equity.
response.population: Studies and statements about adult intensive care patients ventilated or admitted for at least 48 hours and their relatives, published from 2005 to 2026, of any design, in English or with an available translation.
response.exposure: Diaries written wholly or mainly by relatives during the intensive care stay; staff-written and mixed diaries are included as comparators and reported separately.
response.procedures: Search of three bibliographic databases and two guideline repositories with the hospital librarian in October 2026, plus citation chasing from the included review and consensus statement. The clinical nurse specialist screens titles and abstracts; the unit's nurse educator checks a random 20 percent of exclusions and all inclusions. A fixed charting form records design, who wrote, timing and support of reading, outcomes, instruments, harms and delivery features. Synthesis is thematic, with a table of effect estimates as reported and a certainty statement for each conclusion.

outcomes.measure: As reported, with bereaved relatives charted separately

outcomes.why: Relatives write the diaries and carry their own post-intensive care burden.

outcomes.measure: Any reported harm of reading, with timing and support
outcomes.why: Reading is an exposure with a known short-term cost.

outcomes.name: Offer and uptake of diaries
outcomes.measure: Proportion offered and proportion accepting, by language and family presence where reported

response.designSummary: No statistical synthesis: effect estimates are charted and tabulated as reported, with a narrative certainty statement for each conclusion.
response.sampleSize: There is no participant sample. The expected yield is about 15 to 25 records: the eleven controlled studies in the 2023 review, later trials, the harms and uptake studies, and qualitative and consensus work. With three family-written controlled studies measuring different instruments at different times, a pooled estimate would be spuriously precise, so no pooling is planned; the review reports each estimate with its sample size and confidence interval where given.
response.primaryAnalysis: Thematic narrative synthesis under three headings (effects, harms, delivery), with a structured table of reported estimates for the primary outcome by who wrote the diary and when it was read.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Separate tables for relatives, with bereaved relatives apart where reported; a descriptive summary of delivery features and uptake by language and family presence.
response.missingData: Estimates not reported by a study are recorded as not reported, never derived; authors are not contacted within the time available, and this is stated.
response.multiplicity: No hypothesis testing; conclusions are worded by certainty rather than by statistical significance.

Family-written and staff-written diaries kept separate throughout
response.summary: No pooling; reported estimates tabulated with certainty statements.

response.risks: No participants are involved; the risk is a review that overstates benefit and leads the unit to push diaries on families who find them distressing.
response.consent: Not applicable to the review itself; the guideline it informs will describe consent for diary writing, photographs and later reading.
response.data: Only published and publicly available material is used; the unit's uptake figure (118 of 231 families) is quoted in aggregate with the unit manager's agreement.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: families with a different main language, without a regular visitor or able to visit only at night are offered diaries less often. The review reports delivery by these groups where studies allow and recommends translated guides and an offer at the first family meeting.
response.effectiveness: Success is a guideline that uses the review's certainty statements, not a claim that diaries prevent post-traumatic stress.
response.efficiency: Forty hours of existing staff time and a library search; no new cost.
response.costs: Staff time already approved; no purchases.
response.grants: None needed; a later local evaluation of the diary programme could apply to the hospital's nursing research fund.
response.partnerships: Hospital librarian, the unit's nurse educator as second checker, two former patients and one relative from the follow-up clinic's advisory group to read the draft.
response.rebPath: No research ethics review is needed for a review of published literature; if the unit later evaluates its own programme with patient data, that work goes to the research ethics board.
response.limitations: A narrative review, even structured, is more open to selective emphasis than a systematic review; one main reviewer; English-language bias.
response.summary: No participants; equity reporting by language and family presence; research ethics review only for any later local evaluation.

response.title: Family-led intensive care diaries and post-intensive care syndrome in patients and relatives: a narrative review
response.abstract: Diaries written during intensive care are offered to help survivors make sense of memory gaps. This narrative review, based on a documented librarian-supported search and reported against SANRA, summarises evidence on diaries written mainly by relatives: effects on post-traumatic stress, anxiety and depression in patients and relatives, harms of reading, and how programmes are delivered. Results and conclusions will be written after charting.
response.introduction: Post-intensive care syndrome affects survivors and relatives. Diaries are widely used, but clinicians disagree about their benefit, and most studies do not separate family-written from staff-written entries.
response.methods: Search of three databases and two guideline repositories in October 2026 with a librarian, citation chasing, one screener with a second checker for 20 percent of exclusions, a fixed charting form and thematic synthesis with a table of reported estimates. No pooling.
response.results: Not yet written. The section will present the flow of records, the charted studies by design and by who wrote the diary, reported estimates for patients and relatives, harms of reading and delivery features.
response.discussion: The discussion will state what can and cannot be concluded about family-written diaries, give practice points on reading support and equity of offer, and name the evidence that would change the guideline.
response.limitations: Narrative synthesis with one main reviewer; English-language search; few studies of family-written diaries.
response.conclusion: To be written after charting; it will be worded by certainty and will not state that diaries prevent post-traumatic stress.
response.summary: SANRA-structured draft with results left empty until charting is complete.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am the clinical nurse specialist for the ICU follow-up clinic at a regional hospital with a 24-bed mixed medical and surgical intensive care unit. Since March 2025 the families of patients ventilated for more than 72 hours have been offered a paper diary to write in each day, with a one-page guide on what to write and a nurse who checks in twice a week. About half of eligible families take one. At our 3-month follow-up clinic we see patients with nightmares, flashbacks and gaps in memory, and relatives who say they cannot stop replaying the admission.

The unit's education committee has asked me to write a narrative review of family-led diaries and post-intensive care syndrome, in patients and in relatives, to support a unit guideline and a teaching day in spring 2027. I want to know whether diaries written mainly by families, rather than by staff, change post-traumatic stress, anxiety and depression symptoms; when the diary should be read with the patient; what harms have been reported (distress on reading, privacy, photographs); and how diary programmes are run in practice, including who gets offered one.

I also want the review to be honest about how strong the evidence is, because some colleagues treat diaries as proven and others see them as a nice extra. The work has to fit protected time and the hospital library service, with no research funding.
